To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the risk of TB infection in patients receiving anti‐TNFs is high in Asia.
anti‐TNF agents are not contraindicated for patients with IBD in countries with high TB prevalence, but a risk‐benefit analysis is required.
anti‐TNF agents are associated with a small but significant increase in risk of TB, and the risk is higher in Asian patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: 1) the development of consensus statements about the risk assessment, detection and prevention of latent tuberculosis infection and management of TB infection in patients receiving anti-TNF therapy, 2) the quality of the evidence and the strength and the quality of the recommendations were assessed by the Grading of Recommendation Assessment, Development and Evaluation methodology, 3) a web-based consensus vote was conducted among 211 IBD experts from nine Asian countries.

the development of a set of consensus recommendations on the risk assessment, detection and prevention, and management of active tuberculosis infection in patients receiving anti‐tumour necrosis factor therapy.

the following issues: (i) the risk of TB infection among patients with IBD who receive anti‐TNF; (ii) screening of patients prior to commencing treatment with anti‐TNF and the need for preventive treatment; and (iii) the management of patients with latent or active TB.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
patients with latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) should be screened for LTBI prior to starting anti‐TNF, and those with LTBI should receive treatment for LTBI.
anti‐TNF use is associated with a small but significant increased risk of active TB infection.

patients who are at high risk of developing TB infection, including those from countries with a high incidence of TB, those who have been exposed to a person with active TB or who have been in close contact with a person with active pulmonary TB, and those with a history of active TB should be screened for TB prior to commencing therapy with anti‐TNF agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anti‐TNF agents are effective in treating IBD.
the risk of TB infection is increased in IBD patients receiving anti‐TNFs, and that screening for TB infection is mandatory before starting anti‐TNF.
anti‐TNF use in Asian countries should be restricted to patients who have a low risk of TB infection and who have been screened and tested for latent TB infection (LTBI).
The main takeaway from our work is that
all patients with IBD should be screened prior to commencing treatment with anti‐TNF agents.
all anti‐TNF‐naive IBD patients should be screened for latent tuberculosis infection prior to starting anti‐TNF.
clinicians should screen for TB infection in patients who are candidates for anti‐TNF‐based therapy.
